newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Kuchma sets Ukraine new economic course - diplomats.
newsitem.headline: Kuchma sets Ukraine new economic course - diplomats.

text.p: President Leonid Kuchma's fiery address to the Ukrainian nation set a new course for the struggling economy on Friday and served to strengthen his position at the helm of the former Soviet republic, Western diplomats said.
"He showed he really wants to act and is ready to face opposition from communists," one diplomat said. "He showed he is at the centre of all the action."

The 90-minute speech delivered blistering criticism for what he called a lack of responsibility in the government and parliament, aiming several barbs against Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko and his 10 months in office.

"He made a policy speech that seemed to open the election battle," said a diplomat about 1999 presidential elections which will probably be contested by Kuchma, a former missile factory boss who became prime minister in 1994.

Kuchma chided government and parliament for being too slow to pass the 1997 budget, the delay of which, along with a package of tax reforms, has pushed back a badly-needed multi-billion-dollar International Monetary Fund credit.
"The price of these political games is extremely high, and I have no other word but 'game' for what is going on," Kuchma said, adding that the country was in financial chaos.

One diplomat said Kuchma's comments hit on weak spots which have led to a forecast of zero growth this year -- the best Ukraine would do since independence in 1991 -- and a 4.2 billion hryvnia ($2.3 billion) wage debt.

"He called for a better relationship between government and parliament. He beat up on those responsible for the wage arrears problem, which are the enterprises that are not paying the people, and also not paying their taxes," the diplomat said.
"He also talked about the high level of corruption in government, and the need to break down large monopolies."

The diplomat said the speech fell short by not talking about military, education, and health reform -- all have suffered since Ukraine began the long road to a market economy with Kuchma's economic reform programme launched in 1994.
"It's interesting he didn't mention anything about foreign policy, or anything about Russia," another diplomat said.

Ukrainian-Russian relations have been far from warm lately and a post-Soviet friendship treaty has been held up by disagreements between the neighbouring Slav states over the fate of the Black Sea Fleet on Ukraine's Crimea peninsula.
Unlike previous occasions Kuchma refrained from criticising the central bank, whose tight monetary policies helped cut inflation to 39.7 percent last year from 10,225 percent in 1993.
The leader of parliament's Reform Party Serhiy Teryokhyn welcomed Kuchma's comments on the bank, including ones opposing the idea of direct financing to the government and for a currency corridor.

"Kuchma's statements were opposite to Economy Minister Yuri Yekhanurov's most recent statements saying the national bank has to be made to follow government policies, or the prime minister saying there is not enough money in the economy," he said.

The diplomat said Lazarenko's job was likely not in trouble, even though his impending sacking has been widely rumoured in local media. "It is a clear sign to Lazarenko that he has to get in line with the president and not against him," he said.
